tools.name: ECC
tools.what: 299k-star agent harness: 314 skills, 71 agents, 98 commands (plan→code→test→review)
tools.why: Real and huge, but the useful parts are the skills — 12 imported as Hermes skills and all 483 items catalogued. Re-checked 2026-11-08 after @moeen_valpr's reel (cover claims 290K★; actual 299,217, so the claim is honest): upstream advanced 6 commits since b38be6a but only CI/PR-moderation files — zero skill changes, mirror still current. Not a model upgrade; gain is phase discipline + checklists.

tools.name: ascii.rest
tools.what: 240 animated ASCII pieces for the web, one <ascii-art> tag, MIT
tools.why: Wired in: ascii_bumper.mjs captures any piece in headless Chrome and encodes an MP4 — a 2.5s vertical 1080x1920 bumper renders in 2.5s. Used as the short intro; page also renders live for landing pages.

tools.name: StableGen
tools.what: Blender add-on: prompt to textured, rigged 3D character (TRELLIS.2 + SkinTokens + Marigold)
tools.why: Needs Blender plus a ComfyUI GPU server; no /dev/dri here. One rented GPU hour could ship a brand mascot without buying hardware.

tools.name: ClaudeAnimationBase
tools.what: Clawd character kit for p5.brush: 31 acted emotions, an 11s demo, ANIMATION_GUIDE
tools.why: Split verdict: 17.8s per 1280px still makes it a thumbnail/painting tool today (wired in the playbook), while its own video path costs ~19s/frame — a 11s clip is an 80-minute overnight job.

tools.name: huashu-art-motion
tools.what: Claude skill collection for hand-drawn and painterly motion
tools.why: MIT and small; the p5.brush watercolour path costs ~40 s/frame here, so use it for keyframes only.

tools.name: anidoodle
tools.what: Animated doodle/sketch skill for Claude
tools.why: Apache-2.0, ~1.2k stars, lighter than p5.brush; candidate for short-form illustration once tested end to end.

tools.name: code-animation-prompts
tools.what: 341 code-rendered animation styles with prompts
tools.why: Mirrored to workspace/animation-styles and published as code-animation-atlas; 28 runnable on Canvas + headless Chrome with no GPU.

tools.name: TwinDesk
tools.what: Share mouse, keyboard, files and clipboard across machines (KVM)
tools.why: Needs a human at a physical desk; does nothing for a headless server fleet. fleet.py already syncs and dispatches over ssh.

tools.name: FloMorphic getting-started
tools.what: Low-code graph platform for agent pipelines, MCP + RAG + human oversight
tools.why: Eight repos at 0-1 stars, commercial licence, no runnable core — a landing page, not a platform yet.

tools.name: TWP-CF
tools.what: Telegram web proxy on Cloudflare Workers (MTProto over websocket)
tools.why: 11 stars, custom licence and a security warning in its own README; Telegram Web already reaches us from Iran via the existing tunnel.

tools.name: tree-of-neuron
tools.what: Interactive 47-milestone history of neuroscience
tools.why: Nice one-off educational toy, 1 star, no licence; nothing to reuse in our pipeline.

tools.name: Masque Config Generator
tools.what: One-page generator for Xray WARP-over-MASQUE configs (P-256 keys)
tools.why: Technically correct (MASQUE on TCP/443, H2 default for MCI, 162.159.198.0/24 for Irancell) but its fallback posts to an unknown Worker — generate keys locally with usque instead.

tools.name: usque
tools.what: Open-source Cloudflare WARP MASQUE client
tools.why: Local key generation and a real client — the safe half of the MASQUE generator workflow; 1.5k stars, MIT.

tools.name: llama.cpp
tools.what: CPU/GPU inference for GGUF models
tools.why: Runs on this box (build b12064); 0.8B-2B models are usable for batch work, 30B on 6 cores gives 2 tok/s and is not.

tools.name: Muse-Glimmer-30B
tools.what: Apache-2.0 27.85B MoE GGUF, Q4_K_M 16.76 GB
tools.why: Measured on ki: 8.5 tok/s prompt, 2.07 tok/s generation, 28.6 GB peak RAM with default context — overnight batch only, never interactive.

tools.name: OpenCut
tools.what: Browser timeline video editor (CapCut alternative)
tools.why: 97k stars but a GUI timeline for humans; our videos are rendered from code, so an editor adds a step without adding capability.

tools.name: VoiceStudio
tools.what: Local voice cloning and dubbing (ElevenLabs alternative)
tools.why: 100k stars, AGPL; needs GPU/Apple Silicon. The moment the rig exists this is the German voice for DOPEAK.

tools.name: Cal.com (cal.diy)
tools.what: Self-hosted scheduling pages (Calendly alternative)
tools.why: MIT and real, but it wants a domain, TLS and email before it is useful — worth it when the IT work gets its own booking link.

tools.name: AppFlowy
tools.what: Self-hosted Notion alternative
tools.why: Desktop-plus-server product for teams of humans; our notes are markdown in the vault and the bots already read them.

tools.name: Plane
tools.what: Self-hosted Jira/Linear alternative
tools.why: Postgres plus Redis plus a worker; too much server for one person's task list. The kanban tool in Hermes already covers it.

tools.name: Chatwoot
tools.what: Self-hosted Intercom alternative
tools.why: No OSI licence, and a support inbox only pays off after there are customers to support.

tools.name: Cap
tools.what: Open-source Loom alternative for screen recording
tools.why: Non-OSI licence and a desktop app; screen capture on a headless server is ffmpeg, which we already use.

tools.name: Dyad
tools.what: Local Lovable-style app builder
tools.why: Non-OSI licence, GUI-first; writing the code directly with an agent is faster than clicking a builder.

tools.name: OpenSEO (claim)
tools.what: Supposed free Semrush alternative from the same carousel
tools.why: No repository at the claimed size — the name lands on a 2016 and a 2023 project, and the only live one has 27 stars and a week of history.

tools.name: OpenWhispr (claim)
tools.what: Supposed open-source Wispr Flow dictation app
tools.why: Claim did not survive a repo search; no canonical project found to install.

tools.name: Weight-Space Programming
tools.what: MIT CSAIL experiment: an LLM edits another model's raw weights to fix reasoning loops
tools.why: Artifacts are real (logs, edited Qwen3.5-0.8B, eval files) but the headline 6x compares 25 base problems against 500 edited ones, with 95% of base outputs truncated — direction yes, multiplier no. Needs the unreleased GPT-6 Astra.

tools.name: Cinemap
tools.what: 3D previs from text: build an editable set, keyframe props/actors, phone-as-camera via QR, then hand the clip to Seedance 2.5 as a camera reference
tools.why: Real product (cinemap.video, run by TapNow). Pricing now verified via the TapNow pricing page: Basic $15/mo ($7.5/mo billed yearly, 1500 Tapies), Pro $60/mo (6000, top-up $1=107), Ultimate $360/mo, Max $720/mo; 1 Tapie ≈ $0.01 of credit. The camera-reference trick works because Seedance 2.5 ships camera-perspective reference (ByteDance launch post, 2026-07-31). Parked, not skipped: it targets cinematic previs, not our chart-driven shorts, and the reel is a paid ad. Revisit for a film-style piece.

tools.name: ClipUtils
tools.what: 32 browser tools: trim/compress/convert, remove music keeping the voice, auto subtitles, video translation/dubbing, TTS, HEIC/WebP conversion, background removal
tools.why: Real and genuinely free at the core: no signup, no watermark on local tools, and trimming/compressing/converting/removing music run on-device (nothing uploaded). The 'free' claim has limits the homepage buries: video translator 8 min, dubbing 2 min and German is Pro-only, auto subtitles 15 min, TTS 5 min, Text-to-Video adds a cliputils tag. Pro is cheap ($1.49/mo most countries, $2.99 US/Europe). No API, so it cannot be automated into our pipeline. For Ahmad's phone it is a useful one-off tool (remove music, Dub German); for the channel pipeline ffmpeg/whisper/edge-tts stay the answer.

tools.name: AgentPilot
tools.what: 9B strategy model that picks the next move for a bigger agent, plus a skill workspace and an RSI benchmark arena
tools.why: Real (7.9k stars, MIT, HKUDS, pushed 06.11.2026) and it lists Hermes as a supported executor, so the hook exists. But it optimises *improvement policy* over many trials on benchmarks (AIME, SWE-bench, BrowseComp) and needs the 9B policy model itself — on this CPU-only box that means either a slow local model or a second API bill. Our bottleneck is content and distribution, not search over strategies; the honest use case is auto-tuning the render/upgrade loop once the GPU rig exists. Revisit then; not a dependency now.

tools.name: LivLiv Player
tools.what: 2.5D avatar player for the web: WebGL2, ~30KB core, lip sync + MediaPipe face tracking in-browser, VRM/PNGTuber support, 21 sample characters
tools.why: Shipped a real talking-avatar clip on 2026-11-08 (720x1280, 30fps, German VO, Sena/k01) fully headless on CPU via browser_exec + CDP screenshots; skill livliv-avatar-video holds the pipeline. Apache-2.0 core is clean, but the 21 sample characters are non-commercial with a burned-in livliv mark -> monetised channels need our own VRM/PNGTuber. speech.say() does not drive the mouth headless; drive mouthOpen from a Python amplitude envelope. Render speed ~5 fps on CPU (12s clip ~3min).

tools.name: MuJoCo
tools.what: Google DeepMind physics engine (rigid bodies, contacts, actuators): robot sim and physical animation, Python bindings, Apache-2.0
tools.why: Installed 2026-11-08 (pip mujoco 4.0.0) and measured on this CPU-only box: 212,162 steps/s single-thread on a small free-joint scene, so a 6 s 24 fps clip simulates in well under a second. Its own OpenGL renderer does NOT start here (no EGL/OSMesa: 'an OpenGL platform library has not been loaded into this process'), so visuals are drawn from body poses with matplotlib and piped to ffmpeg - that path shipped a 720x1280 domino-chain B-roll clip (out/mujoco-dominoes.mp4). Real use for us: physics-visual shorts for ALGORHYTHM/DOPEAK and validating URDF/MJCF before robot work. Not a CAD/print tool. Reusable CLI now at /opt/data/workspace/physics-broll/render.py (scenes: dominoes, pendulum, balls; 24 fps 720x1280, silent) and it is wired into faceless-youtube/PLAYBOOK.md as a B-roll source.

tools.name: awesome-llm-apps
tools.what: 57 runnable AI app folders (agents, RAG, voice): Streamlit demos, ~17.7k Python lines total, Apache-2.0
tools.why: The reel's claims check out: 144,280 stars (reel said 142K+), Apache-2.0, 100+ apps. But the audit says tutorial-grade: 57 folders with requirements.txt, 45 of them Streamlit, 29 need OpenAI keys, ~310 lines per app on average - demos, not products. The real use for us is the CONTENT mine (each app is a working demo for a 30-45 s short) plus one app productised with auth+billing via stdlib-saas-wrapper, not the whole collection. 'You can sell them' is legally true under Apache-2.0; it is commercially true only with hosting, keys and support. Cloned to /opt/data/workspace/awesome-llm-apps (163 MB).

tools.name: Avatar Creator (AVC Suite)
tools.what: Commercial Blender add-on: build / wrap / sync characters, convert AI meshes and retarget to MetaHuman or Genesis 9
tools.why: Closed-source paid add-on (launch $99, regular $149; bundle with the wrap/sync tool $149 vs $299), sold via Superhive. Relevant to our 3D-avatar plan but blocked on hardware: no Blender on this box, no GPU, 7 GB RAM, and a character pipeline is GPU work. It outputs DCC characters (MetaHuman / Genesis 9), not VRM - our LivLiv PNGTuber path needs VRM or two PNGs, so even with the tool there is an export step. Revisit after the GPU rig; until then LivLiv + our own art stays the cheap route.
